cls: Chelating agent / disease-modifying antirheumatic (copper chelator, thiol)
pharm: Heavy-metal chelator and antirheumatic; reduces cystine excretion
quick: Disease-specific: RA 125-250 mg/day up; Wilson 750-1500 mg/day
Empty stomach, >=1 h before or 2 h after food
Avoid except Wilson's disease/cystinuria; teratogenic risk
summary: Penicillamine is a chelating thiol used in Wilson's disease (copper chelation), cystinuria (reduces urinary cystine to prevent stones) and severe refractory rheumatoid arthritis. Dosing is disease-specific and given on an empty stomach, with pyridoxine supplementation. It is a toxic drug requiring close monitoring: serious haematological reactions (aplastic anaemia, agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia) and renal effects (proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, Goodpasture-like syndrome) can occur at any time, alongside autoimmune syndromes.
indications: Cystinuria (to reduce urinary cystine and prevent/dissolve stones)
Severe active rheumatoid arthritis unresponsive to conventional therapy
Lead and other heavy-metal poisoning (off-label/alternative chelation)

dosage.d: 750-1500 mg/day in divided doses; titrate to cupruresis
dosage.n: Adjust by urinary copper; give pyridoxine 25-50 mg/day
Adjust to keep urinary cystine <100-200 mg/L; high fluids, alkalinise urine

dosage.d: Start 125-250 mg/day; increase by 125-250 mg every 1-3 months to 500-750 mg/day
dosage.n: Max usually 1000-1500 mg/day; slow titration to limit toxicity

admin: Give on an empty stomach, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals
Give at least 1 hour apart from other drugs, food, milk or antacids
For cystinuria maintain high fluid intake (>=2 L/day) and consider urinary alkalinisation
Titrate slowly in rheumatoid arthritis to reduce toxicity
moa: Penicillamine is a thiol that chelates copper, lead, mercury and other heavy metals, forming soluble complexes that are excreted in urine (basis of use in Wilson's disease and metal poisoning). In cystinuria it combines with cystine to form a more soluble disulphide, reducing stone formation. In rheumatoid arthritis it has an incompletely understood immunomodulatory effect, including reduction of rheumatoid factor and effects on T-cell function.

absolute: History of penicillamine-related aplastic anaemia or agranulocytosis
Renal insufficiency in patients with rheumatoid arthritis
relative: Concurrent gold therapy, antimalarials, cytotoxic or other marrow-toxic drugs
monitor: CBC with differential and platelet count
Signs of autoimmune or neuromuscular syndromes

preg: Penicillamine is teratogenic (connective-tissue defects, cutis laxa reported). It is contraindicated in pregnant rheumatoid arthritis patients. In Wilson's disease or cystinuria the benefit may justify continued use during pregnancy at the lowest effective dose, under specialist supervision.
lact: Use during breastfeeding is not recommended; safety in the infant has not been established.
renal: Penicillamine can cause proteinuria, haematuria, nephrotic syndrome and Goodpasture-like syndrome. It is contraindicated in renal insufficiency when used for rheumatoid arthritis. Monitor urinalysis and renal function regularly; reduce or stop for significant or progressive proteinuria.
hepatic: Hepatotoxicity (cholestatic and hepatocellular) occurs rarely. Monitor liver function periodically and evaluate for jaundice or rising enzymes.

major: Gold salts, antimalarials, immunosuppressants, phenylbutazone - additive haematological/renal toxicity; avoid concurrent use
Iron salts - markedly reduce penicillamine absorption; separate dosing
moderate: Antacids - reduce absorption; separate by at least 1 hour
Digoxin - penicillamine may reduce digoxin levels
minor: Pyridoxine requirement increased - supplement to prevent deficiency
interactions.food: Take on an empty stomach; food, milk and antacids reduce absorption.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; it may add to gastrointestinal irritation.
interactions.diagnostics: Increases urinary copper/cystine excretion; may cause proteinuria, cytopenias and positive ANA.

monitoring: CBC with platelets every 2 weeks for first ~6 months, then monthly
Urinalysis (protein, blood) on the same schedule
24-h urinary copper (Wilson's) or cystine (cystinuria) to guide dose
Watch for muscle weakness, rash, fever or bruising
counsel: Take on an empty stomach, well apart from food, milk, antacids and other medicines
Take your vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) supplement as prescribed
Report fever, sore throat, easy bruising, bleeding, frothy urine, swelling or new muscle weakness at once
Drink plenty of fluids (especially for kidney-stone prevention)
Do not stop suddenly without advice, especially in Wilson's disease
pk: RA response over weeks to months; cupruresis within days in Wilson's
Plasma peak ~1-3 h after oral dose
Variable, approximately 1.7-7 h (prolonged with repeated dosing)
Sustained metal chelation with regular dosing
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F) in a tight container
pearls: Highly toxic - serious marrow and renal reactions can appear at any time; regular CBC and urinalysis are essential
Always co-prescribe pyridoxine to prevent deficiency
Give on an empty stomach and well apart from iron, antacids and food which impair absorption
Can induce autoimmune syndromes: myasthenia gravis, lupus, pemphigus, Goodpasture-like disease
In Wilson's disease, an early neurological worsening can occur - introduce gradually under specialist care
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and resume the schedule. Do not double the dose. In Wilson's disease avoid prolonged gaps - contact the prescriber if doses are repeatedly missed.
overdose: Acute overdose may cause severe GI symptoms and potentiate toxicity. There is no specific antidote; manage with supportive care, and penicillamine is dialysable. Monitor blood counts and renal function.
